anti_overlap: Does not evaluate FLUX licensing, privacy-gate correctness, or other legal/commercial prerequisites — that is fd-ip-privacy-compliance's territory.
Does not evaluate mobile-app sequencing, day-one consumer activation, or whether API-first defers the ambient channel — that is fd-mobile-subscription-sequencing's territory.
Focuses on whether the API is a sellable, defensible product on its own commercial terms, not on how the tiers are ordered relative to each other.
decision_lens: For every claimed differentiator, ask whether a technically competent buyer could reproduce it themselves in an afternoon with prompting and structured-output tooling — and if so, what is actually being sold is not the differentiator but the memo's own framing of it.
focus: Whether the stateless soundpost API (Option B Tier 1) is a sellable, defensible product given the ablation's own finding that a frontier model improvises the lens equally well, and whether the memo's agent-builder market and pricing evidence would survive contact with a real buyer.
name: fd-api-business-viability
persona: Apply the perspective of a developer-platform / API-product strategist with experience in devtools go-to-market, usage-based pricing, and build-vs-buy analysis from the buyer's side — someone who has watched a technically real feature fail commercially because a buyer could replicate 80% of its value with a system prompt and a JSON schema.
review_areas: Test whether §3's claimed differentiator ("a schema-enforced one-lens-or-none answer, a calibrated refusal to reframe... and a citation into a curated library") survives a build-vs-buy comparison against a buyer using function-calling/JSON mode and a few-shot refusal prompt against a frontier model — the memo asserts this is "a real product for agent builders" without running that comparison.

Examine the market-sizing gap: §3 and §4 Option B both name "agent builders" as the Tier 1 buyer, but §4's own risk line says "agent builders are a thin market" — no sizing, reachability, or willingness-to-pay evidence is given for either claim, and the memo doesn't reconcile the contradiction.

Stress-test the §7 falsification tests as evidence-generating: does a two-week landing-page waitlist actually distinguish "thin market" from "wrong channel, wrong price, or no launch audience" — a common false negative in early devtools pricing tests — and is a blind preference test among ten FLUX readers (a consumer audience) the right instrument for an agent-builder B2B claim at all.

Check whether Tier 1's commercial claim is being sold ahead of its evidence: the ablation CI-excludes-0.5 result and 0-lens-gate precision are cited in §2.1 as established, but gold_v2 sits at 5 of a needed 40 rows (§2.2, §5), and §5 itself says the API "cannot be marketed on selection quality until gold_v2 crosses 40 rows" — verify Tier 1's "weeks" timeline in §4 doesn't ship before that evidence exists.

Assess Option C's open-core economics: giving the full core (persona, library, schema, eval) away in the free self-hosted tarball tier, described as "the strongest privacy story the seal can offer" (§4 Option B), while charging for a stateless hosted wrapper over the same core — does the memo name a reason a technical buyer picks paid over self-hosting, or does the free tier cannibalize the willingness-to-pay of exactly the technical audience most likely to buy Tier 1.

Identify a cheaper or faster validation the memo omits: e.g., pre-selling Tier 1 to the existing Hermes-user base (a warm, already-adopting audience) before or alongside cold agent-builder outreach — check whether the memo's sequencing forfeits a lower-cost test in favor of the landing-page-only approach in §7.

severity_examples.condition: The recommendation's timeline (§4-5) does not gate Tier 1's public launch or marketing copy on the labeling program actually crossing 40 rows first.
severity_examples.scenario: Tier 1 ships in "weeks" and is marketed to agent builders as "structured, restrained, cited" before gold_v2 reaches the 40-row threshold the memo's own §5 says is required before any selection-quality claim can be made, so the product launches on an evidentiary basis the memo elsewhere states is insufficient.

severity_examples.condition: No market-sizing, reachability, or willingness-to-pay evidence for the agent-builder segment appears anywhere in the memo.
severity_examples.scenario: The memo asserts both that agent builders are the Tier 1 buyer (§3, §4) and that "agent builders are a thin market" (§4 Option B risks) without ever sizing the segment, so mk rules on B without knowing whether Tier 1 can support the API-as-standalone-business framing the recommendation implies.

severity_examples.condition: §4's Option C description names the free tier's privacy strength but doesn't test it against Tier 1's paid conversion assumption.
severity_examples.scenario: Option C's free self-hosted tier is marketed as the strongest privacy story available, which is also the most persuasive reason a privacy-conscious technical buyer — the same profile as an agent builder — would choose not to pay for the hosted API, and the memo doesn't address this tension.

success_hints: Cites specific memo sections (§2.1 ablation, §3 API differentiator paragraph, §4 Option B Tier 1, §5 evidence-base note, §7 falsification tests) rather than generic GTM commentary.
Runs an explicit build-vs-buy test against the claimed differentiator (schema-enforced output, 0-lens gate, citation) rather than accepting that a frontier model can't replicate it.
Treats the gold_v2 5-of-40-rows gap as a live commercial-timing risk for Tier 1, not just a labeling-program status update.
Proposes at least one concrete, cheaper market test the memo's §7 omits (e.g., Hermes-user pre-sell, buyer interviews, open-core cannibalization check).
Distinguishes 'the API can technically be sold' from 'the vision's stated differentiator is provably real' — the memo blurs this distinction in §3.
task_context: This is a pre-ruling stress review of a product-fork memo (`docs/2026-09-03-product-fork-memo.md`) proposing what Auraken should become if mk ships it as a paid mobile app plus an agent/model API endpoint — the memo lays out four options (A: mobile-first; B: API-first, recommended; C: open-core framing of B; D: stay n=1) and asks mk to rule on the audience axis. Stress the memo before mk rules on it: (1) is 'API first, mobile last' actually the pivot-surviving order, or does it defer the only thing (the ambient channel + profile) that makes Auraken more than a system prompt; (2) is a stateless soundpost API a real market for anyone, given the repo's own ablation says a frontier model improvises the lens equally well; (3) what does the memo miss that a paid consumer product for FLUX readers would need on day one; (4) are the FLUX-licensing and privacy-gate claims stated correctly and are there other legal/commercial prerequisites unnamed. Surface missed options and cheaper falsification tests. A wrong ruling here costs months of build on a sixth product shape.
